opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's only new in the sense that the mainstream deep learning community has recently rediscovered it. The idea that you can trade compute at inference time for better performance is very old. Look at AlphaZero or any classical game-playing system: Monte Carlo tree search is test-time compute. Program synthesis has always worked this way. You search over a space of candidate programs at test time, and the more compute you put in, the more of the space you cover and the better your solutions.

What's actually new is the realization that the pure pretraining-scaling paradigm, where you make the model bigger, feed it more data, and expect intelligence to emerge, was hitting diminishing returns. We saw that very clearly on ARC. For years, base LLMs scaled up by something like fifty thousand times and barely moved on ARC, going from roughly zero to maybe a few percent. That tells you that memorizing more patterns isn't the same as being able to adapt to novelty.

Then once people started doing test-time adaptation, through test-time training, program search, or chain-of-thought search with verification, performance suddenly jumped. To me that's not a surprise. It's what you'd expect if intelligence is fundamentally about how efficiently you can adapt to something you haven't seen before. If the model is static at inference time, just fetching and replaying stored programs, it can't really deal with novelty. If it can recombine its knowledge on the fly and search for a new solution, now you're getting somewhere.

So I'd frame it this way. The "test-time scaling law" isn't a new law of nature. It's the field acknowledging that you need some form of active, on-the-fly reasoning, and that this reasoning costs compute. The interesting questions now are about efficiency. If you need thousands of dollars of compute to solve a puzzle a child solves in a few seconds, you've found a way to brute-force the problem, but you haven't matched human-level skill-acquisition efficiency. That's the real measure of intelligence, and that's where I think the research frontier is.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd push back a little on the word "new." The idea that you can trade compute at inference time for better results is not a new discovery. It's one of the oldest ideas in AI. Search is test-time compute. Deep Blue was test-time compute. AlphaGo's Monte Carlo tree search, that's the whole point of it: you have a learned prior and a learned value function, and then at test time you spend compute expanding a tree, and the more compute you spend, the stronger you play. That curve, performance versus search budget, has been known for decades.

What is genuinely new is that people are now applying this idea to large language models, and that it works on domains that used to look unsearchable, like open-ended reasoning in natural language. For a long time the dominant paradigm in deep learning was: the model is a static function. You do a single forward pass, you fetch a memorized pattern, you apply it. All of the intelligence, if you want to call it that, was baked in at training time. The model couldn't adapt to novelty at test time at all. And that is precisely why these systems were stuck on things like ARC. ARC is designed so that memorized templates don't help you. You have to synthesize a new program, a new solution, on the fly.

So when I talk about test-time adaptation, what I mean is that the system is doing something more than retrieval when it encounters a problem. It's recombining what it knows, searching over that space of recombinations, and verifying candidates. That's where the capability jump comes from. The o-series models from OpenAI, the test-time fine-tuning approaches that did well in the ARC Prize, program synthesis with an LLM as the generator and a search loop around it: these are all different ways of reintroducing search and adaptation into a paradigm that had thrown it out.

Now, the "scaling law" framing is where I'd be careful. People love a straight line on a log plot. And yes, if you plot accuracy against inference compute for a given model, you'll get a nice-looking curve. But a scaling law in the pretraining sense was supposed to tell you something fairly universal about loss as a function of data and parameters. What you're seeing at test time is much more task dependent. It depends on whether you have a verifier, whether the problem is decomposable, whether the search space is one the model has good priors over. On math and code, where you can check your answer, the curve looks great. On tasks without a clean verifier, it flattens quickly. So I'd describe it as a demonstration that search works, rather than a new law of nature.

And the deeper point for me is that this validates something I've been arguing for years: intelligence is not the size of your pretrained lookup table. It's the efficiency with which you can turn your existing knowledge into a solution for a problem you haven't seen before. Test-time compute is one mechanism for doing that. It's a necessary ingredient. But if you need to spend thousands of dollars of inference to solve a puzzle a human does in a minute, you haven't closed the gap. You've just shown that it can be brute-forced. The real frontier is making that adaptation efficient, and that's still an open problem.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between a new technique and a new observation about how well that technique works. Spending more computation at inference time to get a better answer is a very old idea. That’s essentially what search does: you explore more possibilities, evaluate them, and hopefully find a better solution.

With language models, you can generate multiple candidate answers, or spend more steps working through a problem. These can be useful ways of trading computation for performance. What could be new is a particular training method that makes this tradeoff more effective, or an empirical finding that performance improves predictably over a certain range of compute.

But calling it a scaling law shouldn’t obscure the mechanism. What are you searching over? How do you recognize a good answer? If you have a reliable verifier, additional search can be very powerful. If you don’t, generating more possibilities doesn’t automatically tell you which one is correct. So I’d want to understand those details before treating test-time scaling as a fundamentally new development.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to distinguish between a new capability and a new way of spending compute. The idea that you can get better results by doing more computation at inference time is very old. Search is exactly that. You explore more possibilities, you evaluate them, and hopefully you arrive at a better answer. So in that broad sense, test-time scaling is not a new development.

What’s interesting is making that process work effectively with language models. You can generate candidate solutions, revise them, or train a model to produce intermediate reasoning that helps it solve a problem. That can be a significant practical advance. But calling it a scaling law doesn’t, by itself, tell you what the limits are.

The key question is: what guides the additional computation? If you have a reliable way to recognize progress or verify a solution, search can be very powerful. If you don’t, spending more compute can simply produce more plausible-looking mistakes. So I would look at the mechanism, the reliability of the feedback, and whether the gains transfer to genuinely novel problems. That’s more informative than the label.
